text: Walter Ernest Fawkes (né Pearsall; 21 June 1924 – 1 March 2023), known as Trog when signing cartoons, was a Canadian-British jazz clarinettist and satirical cartoonist. Born in Vancouver, British Columbia, he moved to Britain with his mother, Mabel (née Ainsley), and her new partner Charles Fawkes in 1931, after his father, Douglas Pearsall, a Canadian railway clerk, left the family. Enthused by comic books from a young age, Fawkes left school at 14 with a scholarship to Sidcup Art School, though he left after 18 months due to financial difficulties. During the Second World War, he was initially employed painting camouflage on factory roofs and later worked for the Coal Commission due to a bout of pleurisy that made him unfit for military service. It was during the war that he began playing in jazz bands. In 1944, he joined George Webb's Dixielanders, a revivalist jazz band featuring Humphrey Lyttelton on trumpet, and later followed Lyttelton when he left in January 1948 to form his own band, remaining with him until 1956. The band evolved into a mainstream jazz group, which suited Fawkes, and he continued to play in various bands, including with George Melly and John Chilton in the Feetwarmers in the early 1970s. He based his clarinet style on that of Sidney Bechet and once recorded with him and Louis Armstrong in 1949 as part of Lyttelton's band. He re-united with Lyttelton periodically and remained an amateur musician. In 1942, Fawkes entered an art competition judged by Leslie Illingworth of The Daily Mail, who later found him working at the paper drawing column-breaks and decorative illustrations on his 21st birthday in 1945. He signed his work as "Trog," a name derived from his experiences in underground air-raid shelters during the war, joking that Londoners were becoming troglodytes. In 1949, his comic strip Flook debuted in The Daily Mail, featuring the satirical adventures of a small, furry eponymous hero, initially aimed at children but evolving into a gentle satire of British politics. Flook ran from 1949 to 1984, with Margaret Thatcher calling it "quite the best commentary of the politics of the day." After its cancellation in 1984, Fawkes moved to Robert Maxwell's Daily Mirror, where Flook briefly appeared in the Sunday Mirror before being dropped. Fawkes also produced political cartoons for The Spectator with George Melly, and occasionally contributed to Private Eye and the New Statesman starting in 1962. His position at The Daily Mail as political cartoonist was threatened by the paper's preference for Gerald Scarfe, prompting him to submit work to other publications, including The Observer, where readers complained his royal cartoons were "grossly discourteous to the Queen." When Scarfe left in 1967, Fawkes' role at The Daily Mail became more secure, and he stopped contributing to The Observer in 1968 to focus on The Daily Mail. In 1969, he became the Daily Mail's political cartoonist upon Illingworth's retirement and also took over the role at Punch. In 1971, when The Daily Mail absorbed The Daily Sketch, Sir David English transformed the paper into a tabloid and assigned Stan McMurtry as political cartoonist, dropping Fawkes from his role. He returned to The Observer in 1971 and continued working for Punch. After Flook ended in 1985, he worked briefly for Today and the London Daily News. During the 1980s, he contributed to Punch and Private Eye, and at The Observer drew a pocket cartoon named "mini-Trog." In 1996, he joined The Sunday Telegraph, where he remained until failing eyesight forced him to retire in 2005 at age 81. In 2013, an exhibition of his work was held at the Cartoon Museum of London. In 1949, he married journalist Sandy Fawkes, who later survived an affair with American serial killer Paul John Knowles; they had four children, one of whom died of SIDS. In 1965, he married Susan Clifford, daughter of Australian composer Hubert Clifford, and they had two children. Fawkes died in London on 1 March 2023, at age 98, following a short illness.
